title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
gist: David Baker's University of Washington lab used RFdiffusion2 and ProteinMPNN to design entirely new zinc and cysteine proteases around a minimal catalytic core, then tuned them to cut specific targets including proteins tied to Alzheimer's and frontotemporal dementia. Success rates and activity were modest versus natural enzymes, and therapeutic delivery hurdles remain large.

insights.claim: Researchers from David Baker's lab at the University of Washington used AI protein design to keep only the catalytic core of two protease types and replace the rest of the protein with a de novo design.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: AI-designed enzymes could be tailored to cut arbitrary targets, widening the addressable space for protein therapeutics and industrial enzymes.

insights.claim: The workflow used RFdiffusion2 to build a backbone constrained to hold the catalytic amino acids and a target sequence, then ProteinMPNN to populate it with amino acids compatible with folding, catalysis and target binding.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Names the specific open tools in this design stack that tool vendors and biotech platforms depend on.
insights.locator: The design process started with software called RFdiffusion2

insights.claim: For the cysteine protease the team made 12 backbones with 69 amino acid sets, and for the zinc protease tried 135 designs; AlphaFold3 found nothing in databases resembling them, suggesting they were novel rather than copied structures.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Structural novelty supports the claim of genuine de novo design, relevant to IP and generalization.
insights.locator: The researchers repeated this process dozens of times

insights.claim: Thirteen cysteine protease designs worked, a 19 percent success rate, but all were considerably less active than the natural yeast enzyme used as the model.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Raw AI designs remain well below natural enzymes in activity, so lab screening is still required.

insights.claim: Zinc designs without a modeled water molecule had a 14 of 89 success rate, but designs with a water molecule placed as a design constraint reached 35 of 38.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Adding the right physical constraint raised hit rate dramatically, showing how model constraints drive success.
insights.locator: The zinc project was a bit more complicated

insights.claim: Swapping in alternative amino acids near the active site produced a cysteine protease that accelerated cleavage by a factor of 109 while staying specific, and a zinc v2 that was 30 times more active than the original design and accelerated cleavage by a factor of 1010 (exponents as rendered in the article text).
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Directed mutation after AI design closes much of the activity gap, implying AI plus screening is the practical workflow.
insights.locator: To find out whether this activity could be improved

insights.claim: The team designed zinc proteases that cut proteins associated with Alzheimer's and frontotemporal dementia in cells, though adapting an existing design to a new target failed and required starting the design over.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Retargeting is not plug-and-play, so per-target design effort limits near-term platform economics.

insights.claim: Therapeutic use faces major hurdles: proteins are hard to deliver, can trigger immune responses, and intracellular targets would likely require delivering the gene encoding the protease.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Delivery and immunogenicity, not design, are the bottlenecks to watch for companies commercializing protease therapies.
insights.locator: What do the results tell us?

insights.claim: Current AI design tools are strong at structure but cannot be told to optimize a specific catalytic activity, so designs lack subtle details of evolved enzymes.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Next gains likely come from tools that can encode activity constraints beyond physical location.
insights.quote: the tools are great at structure, but they’re not necessarily great at activity
insights.locator: But we don't, at the moment
